### Opening Script

Welcome everyone to **GitHub Copilot Fundamentals** — the official GH-300 certification course.

Today we are going to cover all seven exam domains end-to-end, from Responsible AI through prompt engineering to privacy safeguards. This is a demo-led session — I will be showing you everything live using a small Python project called **Mergington High School**.

Mergington High is a FastAPI web application that manages extracurricular activities for students — Chess Club, Programming Class, Gym Class. It has a REST API, a simple HTML/JS frontend, and it is the perfect playground for showing how Copilot helps across the entire SDLC.

We will use this project throughout the day for every demo: fixing bugs, generating data, writing tests, using Agent Mode, and more.

### Transition to audience check

Before we dive in, let me get a quick read on the room so I can calibrate. I am going to drop a couple of polls in chat.

info.label: Talking Points

Focus on workflows, not configuration
Deeper execution comes later (AZ-2007)

The exam covers seven skill domains: Responsible AI (15-20%), Copilot Features (25-30%), GitHub Copilot Features (25-30%), Data & Architecture (10-15%), Prompt Engineering (10-15%), Developer Productivity (10-15%), and Privacy & Safeguards (10-15%)
Related Microsoft Learn paths: 'GitHub Copilot Fundamentals Part 1' (6 modules) and 'Part 2' (6 modules)
notes:
### Demo project introduction

All demos today are based on two official GitHub Skills courses and the **Mergington High School** sample project:

- **Getting Started with GitHub Copilot** — covers Ask Mode, inline suggestions, Inline Chat, Agent Mode, Plan Agent, and PR features
- **Customize Your GitHub Copilot Experience** — covers custom instructions, instruction files, prompt files, and custom agents

The Mergington High School app is a FastAPI Python application with:

```python
# In-memory activity database
activities = {
    "Chess Club": {
        "description": "Learn strategies and compete in chess tournaments",
        "schedule": "Fridays, 3:30 PM - 5:00 PM",
        "max_participants": 12,
        "participants": ["michael@mergington.edu", "daniel@mergington.edu"]
    },
    "Programming Class": { ... },
    "Gym Class": { ... }
}
```

This simple structure is perfect because it is immediately understandable, has obvious extension points, and contains a deliberate bug we will fix live.

items: IDE inline suggestions vs Copilot Chat vs Copilot CLI — three distinct surfaces, one AI backbone
Individual vs team productivity — research shows 55% faster task completion and 78% higher success rate with Copilot
GitHub Copilot plans comparison:
Free/Pro: Public code filter, personal use, no content exclusions, no IP indemnity
Business: Adds user management, data excluded from training by default, IP indemnity, content exclusions, SAML SSO, usage metrics
Enterprise: Adds codebase-aware chat, knowledge bases for organizational context, requires GitHub Enterprise Cloud
Agent Mode: understands intent, creates a plan, pulls in context, and takes action
MCP (Model Context Protocol): standardized way to connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, databases, and APIs
Custom agents: defined as .agent.md files in .github/agents/
Pull Request summaries: AI-generated PR descriptions and review
notes:
### Plan comparison talking script

When presenting the three plans, use this framing:

*'If you are an individual developer experimenting — Free or Pro is great. The moment you need **organizational control** — who can use it, what code is excluded, audit logs — you need Business. And if you want Copilot to understand your **entire codebase** through knowledge bases, that is Enterprise.'*

Key differentiator to emphasize: **IP indemnity** only kicks in on Business/Enterprise when the public code filter is set to Block.

### Custom agents & prompt files — from Customize course

Briefly preview what participants will see later:

*'In the Customize course, the Mergington High School teacher creates three types of customization files:'*

1. **`copilot-instructions.md`** — repository-wide context ('this is an educational website for homework assignments')
2. **`.instructions.md`** files — targeted to specific file patterns (e.g., `applyTo: "assignments/**/*.md"`)
3. **`.prompt.md`** files — reusable prompts invoked via `/slash-commands` (e.g., `/new-assignment`)
4. **`.agent.md`** files — custom agents with personality and tool restrictions (e.g., brainstorming-only agent)

This is the customization stack — from broad to specific.

notes:
### Whiteboard / slide script — draw the pipeline

Draw or display this 9-step pipeline. Walk through each box:

```
User types in IDE
  ↓
1. Secure Transmission (HTTPS)
  ↓
2. Context Gathering (code before/after cursor, filename, open tabs, FIM)
  ↓
3. Proxy Filter (blocks prompt injection)
  ↓
4. Toxicity Filter (blocks hate speech, PII)
  ↓
5. LLM Code Generation
  ↓
6. Post-Processing (security checks — XSS, SQL injection)
  ↓
7. Public Code Matching (optional, >150 chars)
  ↓
8. Suggestion Delivered to IDE
  ↓
9. Feedback Loop (accept/modify/reject)
```

**Key talking point:** *'Notice the suggestion passes through TWO filter stages — one before the LLM (steps 3-4) and one after (steps 6-7). This is defense in depth. But neither filter is perfect, which is why human review remains essential.'*

### Concrete example — what context does Copilot see?

Open `app.py` and place the cursor inside the `signup_for_activity` function. Explain:

*'Right now, Copilot is gathering context from: the code before my cursor (the function signature, the activity validation), the code after my cursor (the append call), the filename `app.py`, the file type Python, and any open tabs. If I also have `index.html` and `app.js` open, those provide additional cross-file context.'*

This is why the Skills course step 3 says: *'Open the files related to our webpage then drag each editor window to the chat panel'* — you are manually supplementing the automatic context.

info.label: Talking Points
items: INBOUND FLOW — How your prompt becomes a suggestion:
Step 1 — Secure Prompt Transmission: User prompt sent over HTTPS to GitHub Copilot servers
Step 2 — Context Gathering: Copilot collects code before/after cursor, filename, file type, adjacent open tabs, project structure, and uses Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) technique
Step 3 — Proxy Filter: Prompt passes to proxy server in GitHub-owned Azure tenant; blocks prompt injection and manipulation attempts
Step 4 — Toxicity Filtering: Content filtering blocks hate speech, offensive language, personal data
Step 5 — Code Generation with LLM: Filtered prompt passed to large language models for code generation
OUTBOUND FLOW — How suggestions are validated:
Step 6 — Post-Processing: Toxicity filter removes harmful content; proxy applies quality/security/ethics checks
Step 7 — Public Code Matching (optional): Admin-configurable filter prevents suggestions >150 characters that match public GitHub code — required for IP indemnity
Step 8 — Suggestion Delivery: Only suggestions passing all filters are delivered to user
Step 9 — Feedback Loop: Copilot learns from accepted, modified, and rejected suggestions
Key privacy points: Business/Enterprise data is not used for model training; prompts are not stored beyond the session

notes:
### The 'signup bug' as Responsible AI lesson

The Mergington High School project has a **deliberate bug**: students can register for the same activity more than once. The `signup_for_activity` function simply appends the email without checking for duplicates:

```python
@app.post("/activities/{activity_name}/signup")
def signup_for_activity(activity_name: str, email: str):
    # Validate activity exists
    if activity_name not in activities:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Activity not found")
    activity = activities[activity_name]
    # Add student  <-- NO duplicate check!
    activity["participants"].append(email)
    return {"message": f"Signed up {email} for {activity_name}"}
```

Use this to illustrate: *'If you asked Copilot to generate this signup endpoint from scratch, it might or might not include a duplicate check. The AI does not know your business rules. **You** must validate every suggestion against your requirements.'*

Then show the fix that the Skills course walks through — adding a comment and letting inline suggestions complete it:

```python
# Validate student is not already signed up
if email in activity["participants"]:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Student is already signed up")
```

This is **validation in action** — the developer guided Copilot with a comment, reviewed the suggestion, and accepted it.

info.label: Talking Points
items: Copilot output is not final truth — every suggestion requires human review
Risks: incorrect logic, security gaps, bias in training data, over-reliance, outdated patterns, hallucinated APIs
Microsoft/GitHub Six Principles of Responsible AI:
1. Fairness — AI systems should treat all people fairly
2. Reliability & Safety — AI must operate reliably, respond safely to unexpected conditions
3. Privacy & Security — Respect user privacy, collect only needed data, encrypt appropriately
4. Inclusiveness — AI systems must empower everyone regardless of ability, language, or geography
5. Transparency — Explain how systems operate, be honest about limitations
6. Accountability — AI creators must be responsible for system operation
notes:
### Six Principles — Mergington mapping

Make each principle concrete with the Mergington project:

- **Fairness**: If Copilot generates activity descriptions, check they don't assume gender, ability, or cultural norms
- **Reliability**: The signup endpoint must handle edge cases (empty email, non-existent activity) — test what Copilot generates
- **Privacy**: The `participants` list contains student emails — Copilot should not leak those into logs or error messages
- **Inclusiveness**: The web frontend should be accessible — does Copilot-generated HTML include `alt` text, ARIA labels?
- **Transparency**: When using Agent Mode to implement features, the diff review step (Keep/Discard) is the transparency mechanism
- **Accountability**: The developer who accepts the suggestion owns the code — Copilot does not

notes:
### The 4 S's — use Mergington examples for each

Present each S with a concrete Mergington prompt:

**Single** — one task per prompt:
- ❌ Bad: *'Add activities, fix the bug, and write tests'*
- ✅ Good: *'Add a duplicate-registration check to the signup endpoint'*

**Specific** — explicit details:
- ❌ Bad: *'Add some validation'*
- ✅ Good: *'Add email format validation to signup_for_activity that rejects emails not ending in @mergington.edu'*

**Short** — concise but clear:
- ❌ Bad: A 200-word paragraph describing everything about the signup flow
- ✅ Good: *'Validate that activity has available spots before adding participant'*

**Surround** — provide context through open files and descriptive names:
- Open `app.py`, `index.html`, and `app.js` before prompting about the signup flow
- The filename `app.py` tells Copilot it is Python; the import `from fastapi import FastAPI` tells it the framework

info.label: Talking Points
items: The 4 S's of Prompt Engineering (from Microsoft Learn):
Single — Focus on one well-defined task or question per prompt
Specific — Make instructions explicit and detailed for precise suggestions
Short — Keep prompts concise while being specific
Surround — Use descriptive filenames and keep related files open for context
Learning approaches:
Zero-shot: No examples — rely on Copilot's training alone
One-shot: Single example to guide Copilot for consistent implementations
Few-shot: Multiple examples to balance unpredictability with precision
Advanced prompting techniques:
Role prompting: Instruct Copilot to 'Act as a security expert'
Chain prompting: Build iterative conversations — Turn 1: Create function → Turn 2: Add error handling → Turn 3: Add tests
Context sources Copilot uses: code before/after cursor, filename, open tabs, project structure
notes:
### Zero-shot vs. few-shot — live comparison

**Zero-shot demo** (no examples):
1. In `app.py`, place cursor after the last endpoint
2. Type comment:
   ```python
   # Endpoint to remove a student from an activity
   ```
3. Let Copilot generate — review the result. It should produce a reasonable `DELETE` or `POST` endpoint

**Few-shot demo** (provide pattern):
1. Show Copilot the existing `signup_for_activity` function as the pattern
2. Use Inline Chat (`Ctrl+I`), enter:
   ```
   Following the same pattern as signup_for_activity,
   create an unregister_from_activity endpoint that
   removes a student's email from an activity's participants list.
   Return 404 if activity not found, 400 if student not registered.
   ```
3. Compare: the few-shot version should match the existing error handling style, HTTP status codes, and return message format

**Script:** *'See how providing the existing pattern as context gives us a more consistent result? This is why the Skills course tells you to drag relevant files into the chat panel — you are giving Copilot examples to learn from.'*

### Role prompting demo

In Copilot Chat, enter:

```
Act as a cybersecurity expert.
Review the signup_for_activity function in app.py.
Identify all security vulnerabilities and suggest fixes.
```

Compare with a generic prompt:
```
Review the signup function
```

The role prompt should produce a more thorough analysis: missing input validation, no authentication, no rate limiting, no max_participants enforcement, email injection risk.

**Script:** *'The role prompt changes Copilot's perspective. Same code, same model, but the framing "Act as a cybersecurity expert" activates a different knowledge domain.'*

notes:
### Testing demo overview

This demo follows **Skills Step 4** directly — it uses Plan Agent to create a testing strategy, then hands off to Agent Mode for implementation.

The Mergington project has **zero test coverage** initially. The `pytest.ini` and `requirements.txt` are already configured (pytest, httpx for async testing), but no test files exist.

This is the most impactful demo for enterprise audiences — they care about quality and coverage, not just speed.

info.label: Talking Points
items: Test generation with Copilot — key capabilities:
Generate unit tests from function signatures and behavior
Create realistic test data sets
Identify edge cases that humans often miss
Suggest appropriate assertions based on expected behavior
Fix failing tests by analyzing error messages
Plan Agent workflow for testing:
1. Start with broad request → Plan Agent researches and drafts plan
2. Refine with follow-up prompts (testing pattern, framework)
3. Review plan → Click Start Implementation → Agent Mode executes
4. Agent Mode creates files, runs tests, fixes failures in a loop
notes:
### Test categories to expect

When Plan Agent generates a testing plan for the Mergington API, expect these test categories:

1. **GET /activities** — returns all activities with correct structure
2. **POST /activities/{name}/signup** — happy path, successful signup
3. **POST /activities/{name}/signup** — 404 for non-existent activity
4. **POST /activities/{name}/signup** — 400 for duplicate registration
5. **GET /** — redirects to static HTML

The AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) pattern from the Skills course:
```python
def test_signup_success(client):
    # Arrange
    activity = "Chess Club"
    email = "newstudent@mergington.edu"
    
    # Act
    response = client.post(f"/activities/{activity}/signup?email={email}")
    
    # Assert
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert email in activities[activity]["participants"]
```

notes:
### Content exclusion scenario — Mergington example

Use the Mergington project to illustrate content exclusions:

*'Imagine the Mergington school stores student grades in a `grades/` directory alongside the activity code. The school does not want Copilot to ever read or suggest code based on grade data. An admin would configure a content exclusion rule for `grades/**` at the organization level.'*

What happens when exclusion is active:
- No inline completions in excluded files
- Excluded files cannot be referenced in chat
- Content from excluded files is not sent as context for other files

**Script:** *'This is not about Copilot being unsafe — it is about defense in depth. Even though Business/Enterprise data is not used for training, content exclusions ensure sensitive files are never even sent to the LLM for processing.'*

info.label: Talking Points
items: Content Exclusions (Business/Enterprise only):
Admins can configure Copilot to ignore specific files or repositories
Excluded files: no completions, cannot be referenced in chat, not included in context for other files
Configured at repository or organization level
Matching Public Code filter:
Identifies and filters suggestions >150 characters matching publicly available code on GitHub
Organization admins (Business/Enterprise): can block for all members — required for IP indemnity
Personal users (Free/Pro): can toggle Allow/Block in Settings
IP Indemnity (Business/Enterprise only):
Provides legal protection against intellectual property claims
Requirement: Matching public code setting must be set to 'Block'
GitHub assumes legal responsibility if a suggestion infringes third-party IP
Audit Logs:
Available on Business/Enterprise plans for tracking Copilot usage
REST API available for managing subscriptions and usage metrics
Ownership of outputs: generated code suggestions — understand limitations and legal considerations

notes:
### Customization walkthrough — from Customize Skills course

Show each file type from the Customize course with Mergington examples:

**1. Repository instructions** (`copilot-instructions.md`):
```markdown
# Project Description
This project is an educational website for sharing homework
assignments and coding exercises with students.

## Project Guidelines
- Maintain consistent styling across all pages
- Keep file and folder names descriptive and organized

## Educational Standards
- Learning-focused: clear learning objectives
- Student-friendly: clear, encouraging language
```

*'This file is like a README for Copilot. It is automatically included in every chat request.'*

**2. Targeted instructions** (`.instructions.md`):
```yaml
---
applyTo: "assignments/**/*.md"
---
```
*'This only applies when Copilot works on assignment markdown files. You would not want assignment formatting rules polluting Python code suggestions.'*

**3. Prompt files** (`.prompt.md`):
*'Type `/new-assignment` in Agent Mode and Copilot follows a multi-step workflow: create directory, create README from template, update config.json. Repeatable automation.'*

**4. Custom agents** (`.agent.md`):
*'The brainstorming agent has a defined personality (short responses, always ends with a question) and restricted tools (search, web only — no file editing). It is a specialized conversation mode.'*

notes:
### Measurement framework — four stages explained

Present as a maturity curve:

```
Stage 1: Evaluation   → Leading indicators: satisfaction, Daily Active Users, Acceptance Rate
Stage 2: Adoption     → Productivity metrics, enablement, training needs via API
Stage 3: Optimization → Fine-tune for org goals, reduce time-to-market
Stage 4: Sustained    → Continuous monitoring, evolve as org changes
```

**Script:** *'Most organizations I work with are in Stage 1 or 2. The key metrics at that stage are Daily Active Users (are people actually using Copilot?), Acceptance Rate (are they accepting the suggestions or dismissing them?), and developer satisfaction surveys.'*

### REST API example

```
GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/usage
```

Returns daily breakdown of: suggestions made, suggestions accepted, active users — sliced by editor (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains) and language (Python, JavaScript, etc.).

*'If you see high usage in Python but low acceptance in Java, that tells you Copilot works well for Python in your codebase but may need better context setup for Java projects.'*

info.label: Talking Points
items: Measurement Framework — four stages:
1. Evaluation: focus on leading indicators — developer satisfaction, Daily Active Users, Acceptance Rate
2. Adoption: monitor productivity metrics and enablement indicators; identify training needs via API insights
3. Optimization: fine-tune impact on organizational goals
4. Sustained efficiency: continuously evaluate as organization evolves
REST API for usage metrics: available at enterprise, organization, and team levels
GitHub Copilot Developer Survey:
Short-form: every 2 weeks — overall satisfaction, challenges, time saved
Long-form: every 4 weeks — deeper analysis of team dynamics, usage patterns
Research results: developers completed tasks 55% faster and had 78% higher success rate
